title: Shakespeare’s riot of humanity
gist: Jonathan Esty argues that the viral Ian McKellen reading of Sir Thomas More's pro-stranger speech distorts its context: the play sympathised with the anti-foreigner rioters, and More's speech is a sermon on obedience to the king, as in early modern Europe toleration of outsiders came from royal dispensation rather than popular sentiment.

themes.theme: Classics and Shakespeare in migration politics

insights.claim: Christopher Nolan's Odyssey (July) renders xenia, the bond between host and guest, as 'Zeus's law' and its message is that a society that cannot keep the law of hospitality will not survive; it was released amid elections dominated by immigration and deportations.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Cultural products are being read as commentary on migration politics.
insights.locator: Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, released in July

insights.claim: Sweden's centre-right government was narrowly ousted in September in an election fought over deportations and asylum caps, and US voters go to the polls in November with immigration enforcement looming over political debate.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Immigration remains the dominant electoral issue across democracies in autumn 2026.
insights.locator: In September, Swedes narrowly ousted their centre-right government

insights.claim: Sir Ian McKellen performed More's speech on The Late Show, ending with 'William Shakespeare, 400 years ago', and the clip went viral, inviting the audience to see Shakespeare as an early opponent of xenophobia.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Example of the use of canonical authors as proxies in current political fights.

themes.theme: What the original play actually says

insights.claim: The censor was frightened by Sir Thomas More not for its tolerance but for its sympathy for the xenophobic rioters, and the speech McKellen performed is a sermon promoting obedience to the king.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Popular modern readings invert the original political content; check primary texts before using as evidence.
insights.quote: What frightened the censor about the original play
insights.locator: The manuscript of Sir Thomas More tells a very different story

insights.claim: Master of the Revels Edmund Tilney ordered the text to 'Leave out the insurrection wholly and the cause thereof', and the play was never printed and apparently never performed in its day.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Documented censorship shows what authorities feared: depicting popular anti-foreigner unrest.
insights.quote: Leave out the insurrection wholly and the cause thereof.
insights.locator: Edmund Tilney, the Master of the Revels

insights.claim: The play dates from the early 1590s, when Londoners were seething at Protestant refugees from the Low Countries and France accused of undercutting English craftsmen, and a May 1593 libel on the Dutch Church wall said 'ye strangers' beggared honest Englishmen.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Economic competition anxiety about immigrants has deep historical precedent.
insights.locator: The original play dates to the early 1590s

insights.claim: The 'strangers' who actually appear in the play are rich, obnoxious Lombards, not sympathetic refugees, while the rioters are portrayed as hot-headed and a bit silly but fundamentally decent, with real wrongs.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: The play gave xenophobes easy targets rather than sympathetic outsiders.
insights.locator: Worse than that, the play gives the xenophobes easy targets

insights.claim: The only three surviving pages in Shakespeare's own hand rewrite the riot climax, give the mob the best jokes, and complain of the cost of living (butter at elevenpence a pound, meal at nine shillings a bushel), echoing the real 1593 libel's complaint about rents.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Cost-of-living grievances are central in the historical anti-immigrant mobilisation.
insights.locator: The only three pages of the play that survive in Shakespeare’s own hand

insights.claim: More's speech makes an empathy appeal but its core is Tudor political theology: rioters sin by sitting as kings in their desires, and strangers are to be spared because the king has chosen to shelter them, so defying the king is treason and impiety.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Toleration is framed as top-down grant, not popular rights.

insights.claim: In early modern Europe the toleration of outsiders was usually a royal dispensation granted by rulers who prized the skills, capital and taxes strangers brought, and was resented by lower orders who had to compete with them.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Elites tolerate immigration when it is economically useful, while lower-income groups bear competition costs; a recurring political cleavage.
insights.quote: In early modern Europe, the toleration of outsiders was usually a royal dispensation
insights.locator: None of that makes Shakespeare a xenophobe

insights.claim: Edward VI chartered London's first Stranger Church in 1550, and Elizabeth's Privy Council shielded Dutch and French Protestants from the City's guilds and apprentices.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Concrete historical examples of royal protection of immigrant groups against guild pressure.
insights.locator: Edward VI chartered London’s first Stranger Church

insights.claim: Cosmopolitanism has often been unpopular and elitist while nativism has often been popular, not just populist, and strangers have been safest when authority found them useful.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Pro-immigration positions lacking elite backing are politically fragile; expect cycles of backlash.
insights.quote: cosmopolitanism has often been unpopular and elitist, and nativism has often been popular, not just populist

insights.claim: Later reworkings of Thomas More vary by era: Robert Bolt's 1960 A Man for All Seasons makes him a noble martyr for conscience, Hilary Mantel's Wolf Hall makes him a joyless zealot, and McKellen's version makes him a welcomer of the stranger, while the historical More was humanist, persecutor and martyr at once.
insights.speaker: Jonathan Esty
insights.so_what: Historical figures are repeatedly reshaped to suit present arguments.
insights.locator: McKellen’s version is far from the first More revivified
